title: Venus Flytraps: Plant or Monster?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Venus flytrap: its carnivorous habit, why it evolved to eat insects (nutrient-poor wetland soil), the Carolina home range, the origin and controversial history of its name (Venus, folklore of the vagina dentata, the alternate name Diana mousetrap, the English nickname "tippity witch"), Darwin's praise, and how the trap works (trigger hairs, action potentials, closing, sealing with cilia, digestion over days, reset). They discuss whether plants think, then give tips on growing a Venus flytrap at home (distilled or rainwater, bottom watering, winter dormancy, feeding freeze-dried insects). Episode ends with a listener mail about "clarking" someone and a tangent about celebrity anecdotes.

segments.title: Opening banter and plant intelligence
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, joke about breatharians and WKRP, and discuss whether plants think, citing action potentials in Venus flytraps.

segments.title: Carnivorous plants and the Little Shop of Horrors name
segments.summary: Venus flytraps are one of many carnivorous plants but get the most attention. Hosts discuss the Audrey II reference and a Carolina spider trap nickname, the plant's small native range along the Carolinas, and its bog habitat.

segments.title: Origin of the name and folklore
segments.summary: Hosts explain the name's origin, linked to Venus and the vagina dentata folklore, and mention the English nickname tippity witch, Darwin's praise, and the taxonomic name Dionaea muscipula meaning mousetrap, linked to Diana.

segments.title: Why the plant eats insects
segments.summary: Because its wetland soil lacks nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients, the plant gets amino acids, vitamins, and minerals from insects. It still photosynthesizes for sugars and energy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the trap mechanism discussion.

segments.title: How the trap closes
segments.summary: Insects touching trigger hairs start a timer; a second touch within about 20 to 30 seconds closes the lobes in a fraction of a second. Scientists have a hypothesis involving water pressure changes in cells and action potentials. Cilia interlock to form a sealed cage.

segments.title: Digestion, false alarms, and lifespan
segments.summary: The trap seals in an hour or two, resets after about twelve hours for false alarms, and digests prey over five to twelve days. Trigger hairs gauge prey size so the plant releases just enough enzymes. Each lobe closes about ten to twelve times before retiring, and plants can live about twenty years.

segments.title: Growing a Venus flytrap at home
segments.summary: Tips for growing one indoors: a terrarium for dry climates, bottom watering with distilled, deionized, reverse osmosis, or rainwater rather than tap water, no fertilizer, a winter dormancy period in cold, and feeding freeze-dried insects with a toothpick to trigger the trap. Propagation by seed or division.

segments.title: Hosts' celebrity anecdotes
segments.summary: Off-topic banter about Pat Morita, Mr. T, Wyclef-style music video shoots, and a Busta Rhymes anecdote.

segments.title: Listener mail: clarking
segments.summary: Listener Leslie writes that she has been using Clark as a verb with her family after a previous episode, and the hosts read the email and thank her.
